title: Ang 94: Majh begins
hookLine: Guru Ram Das opens the raga
tomorrow: what do you write when you miss someone that much?

lines: WHO WOULD YOU GIVE ANYTHING TO MEET?
cards: Ask a group chat who they'd give anything to meet and the answers pour in: a singer, a player, a grandparent who's gone. On ang 94, Majh, the Granth's second raga, opens with Guru Ram Das's answer.
It isn't a well-known name. It's whoever would introduce him to his Beloved.

teach.h: CAN A FRIEND LEAD YOU TO GOD?
teach.b: Here's the question underneath: can a friend lead you to God? Guru Ram Das's first Majh hymn longs for exactly that.

teach.h: MAJH: BRING ME TO MY BELOVED.
teach.b: In paraphrase: if some friend, some saint, would come and bring me to meet my Beloved, I would give myself to them. The longing is for the One. But the road runs through a person.
That's the Sikh picture of sangat, the holy company: the people who make the Name easier to remember, just by being around. Now a neighbor who says something close, in its own words.
In the Buddhist scriptures, the Upaddha Sutta, the Buddha's attendant Ananda says that good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha answers, in paraphrase: don't say that, Ananda.
Good friendship is the whole of the holy life. And the Buddha calls himself that kind of friend to everyone who walks the path.
So two traditions agree that nobody walks this alone; the friend is not a bonus, the friend is the road. And here's the honest difference.
In the sutta, the good friend leads along the noble path, toward freedom from suffering, with no Beloved Lord waiting at the end.
In Majh, the friend's whole job is to bring you to the Beloved, the One the Guru aches to meet. Same road, a different meeting at the end of it.

how: Sikhs speak of the sangat, the holy company at the gurdwara and beyond, as the place where the Name is easier to remember; Majh hymns are sung in kirtan, and readers in order reach them after Sri Rag.

games.q: a friend on the road — tap the pairs.
p: longs for the friend who leads to the Beloved
the holy company that helps you remember
good friendship is the whole of the holy life

s: in the Upaddha Sutta, the Buddha calls good friendship half of the holy life
Ananda says half; the Buddha answers: the whole of it.
Majh opens with Guru Ram Das longing for whoever would bring him to his Beloved
he'd give himself to that friend.
the Sikh and Buddhist teachings say the friend leads to the same meeting
in the sutta the friend leads along the noble path; in Majh, to the Beloved Lord.

games.q: your older brother says needing a mentor means you're weak, and real seekers find God alone. what do Majh and the Upaddha Sutta both say?
o: both say a teacher is for beginners, then you go on alone.
both prize the friend who shows the way; nobody walks it alone.
both say the friend is the same as God.
games.why: Guru Ram Das would give himself to the friend who leads to the Beloved; the Buddha calls good friendship the whole of the holy life. they differ on where the road ends, not on needing company.

practice: If a Gurbani app is open, read the first hymn on ang 94 before you begin.

Count, slowly, on your fingers, the people who have made it easier for you to be good, or to remember what matters: a teacher, a grandparent, a friend who drove you somewhere when you needed it. For each finger, picture a face.
Then rest your hands in your lap and let the sit be gratitude without words.
